item.title: The Invisible Labor That Sustains Relationships
item.description:
Memory

The Invisible Labor That Sustains Relationships

When remembering is a labor of love.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Making plans, reminding others, and completing those plans is the invisible labor of prospective memory.
  • How the demands of memory are distributed in a relationship influences the health of that relationship.
  • Inequitable division of memory labor can cause frustration and stress, especially when unacknowledged.
  • Prospective memory is necessary for the healthy functioning of relationships and families.
Source: Mizuno Kozuki/Pexels

Keeping everyday life running smoothly in families and romantic relationships requires a lot of everyday remembering. In particular, it requires remembering to carry out future activities—appointments, grocery shopping, picking up and dropping off children, meals, meeting a spouse at work, scheduled social gatherings, romantic interludes, running errands.

Such memory for future activities is called "prospective memory," which entails remembering an intention to do something in the future—and then doing it.

To fulfill an intention, we may need to remind ourselves repeatedly before carrying out the intended action. We can also be cued spontaneously. Seeing a neighbor outside, for example, may cue us to remember her package that was mistakenly delivered to our house sitting in our kitchen.

Prospective memory in families and romantic relationships takes place in four stages: 1) planning, 2) reminding ourselves and others, 3) remembering and carrying out the activities, and 4) evaluating how well the activities were completed. This memory work often goes unnoticed by others and can be thought of as invisible labor.

Prospective Memory Load

In a 2022 study, psychologists Erin Harrington and Celinda Reese-Melancon focused on how prospective memory is distributed in households with children—a study with important revelations about this form of invisible labor.1

Parents completed questionnaires about their own prospective memory work and about the prospective memory work of their partner. They also specified how frequently they engaged in each of the four prospective memory stages for their children and their partner—planning, reminding others, remembering to carry out the plans, and evaluating the outcome. Here is what Harrington and Reese-Melancon found.

Source: Ekaterina Bolovtsova/Pexels

Prospective Memory for Children. Fathers viewed the division of memory labor in the family as equitable, whereas mothers judged themselves as carrying more of the cognitive load, particularly with their children.

Interestingly, when mothers judged how much fathers did, that judgment matched up with the fathers’ own judgments. But when fathers judged how much memory work mothers did, the fathers’ judgments fell significantly short of what mothers reported.

Further investigation revealed that mothers do have a heavier load of prospective memory work and that much of this heavier load focuses on the initial stages of prospective memory—planning how and when to complete a future task and then reminding children of the plans. Fathers also do this, but not to the same extent.

Indeed, a study conducted by Lindsey Robertson, Tamara Anderson, and Christina Kim found that mothers work continuously on prospective memory to keep a household running smoothly.

Prospective Memory for One’s Partner. The same pattern showed itself with the amount of memory support parents provided for each other. Fathers judged it as similar, whereas mothers judged that they stepped in significantly more to help the father with his prospective memory tasks.

Source: Ketut Subiyanto/Pexels

Questions and an Answer

Why is there a discrepancy between the fathers’ perceptions of the mothers' memory work and the mothers’ own perceptions of their memory work? More broadly, why is there a difference in memory load for mothers and fathers? These two questions point to the same answer and suggest possible remedies.

One hypothesis is that larger memory loads for mothers arise, to a large extent, from fathers not apprehending how much prospective remembering mothers actually do. Fathers are not knowingly pulling back on their memory responsibilities. They underestimate mothers’ memory load and then do what they think matches the mothers’ efforts.

Source: wwwkaboompics/Pexels

Out of Sight Out of Mind

In a comprehensive study of the kinds of memory work mothers and fathers do, Robertson and her colleagues found the following pattern. The fathers’ prospective memory load involves discrete, observable tasks (remembering to collect and take out the garbage, remembering to mow the lawn), whereas the mothers’ prospective memories involve many small and unobserved tasks (organizing family schedules, keeping track of a child’s medications, remembering to pay bills on time).

In this study, one mother described her responsibilities as a “background job” that needed constant attention. She also reported that when she explained her mental labor in work-related terms, her husband had a better understanding of how often she engaged in her cognitive tasks. This suggests that if fathers cannot actually see how frequently their partners support their own and their child’s prospective memory intentions, then they cannot truly appreciate their partners’ mental labor.

Moving Toward a Balanced Workload With Memory

1) Externalizing Prospective Memory. Rather than relying on spontaneous memory strategies for encoding and retrieval, families can use tools to externalize memory, with centrally located to-do lists, calendars, and chore-boards. These tools make everyone aware of what needs to be done, while taking the pressure off retrieving specific intentions at the right time.

2) Collaborative Remembering. Partners can support each other at each phase of the prospective memory process, beginning with planning. In particular, mothers and fathers can agree to prompt one another along the way, thereby doubling the chances of remembering, while also encouraging collaborative remembering.

Source: Hassan Ouajbir/Pexels

3) Alarm Apps. Apps can support prospective memory by working as scheduled alarms, reminding us of daily obligations that need to be carried out at a particular time.

We can also use location-based alarm apps to remind us of a particular intention when we are at the right place for carrying out that intention. If we are at the grocery store, for example, an alarm can go off based on our phone’s GPS, reminding us to pick up blueberries and heavy cream for dessert.

4) Identifying Smaller Tasks. Chore boards, calendars, and scheduled reminders can help us only if we’ve identified the many informal daily tasks that rely on prospective memory. First, we need to specify and clarify these numerous small tasks.

5) Attending to the Subject of Prospective Memory. It’s helpful to set aside regular meeting times for discussing the prospective memory demands in one’s household. The discussion times should be placed on the calendar, along with the various prospective memory tasks.

Final Words

Being required to plan, to remind your partner and children about the planning, to carry out the plan, and then to evaluate its success all contribute to the invisible load of maintaining romantic relationships and families. Making this invisible labor known and talking about it supports the interactions between mothers and fathers, while nourishing their relationship and the entire family.

item.title: 5 Smart Ways to Hang Out More in the “Now”
item.description:
Cognition

5 Smart Ways to Hang Out More in the “Now”

The present moment is all we have, and spending time here is life-enhancing.

Posted August 3, 2026

Imagine there's no time.
Source: Photo by Susan K. Perry

I’m not a philosopher. I do, however, enjoy having my mind bent briefly into pretzel shapes by reading books by scientists and philosophers who have a knack for writing for broad audiences. I recently dove into such a book, In Search of Now: The Science of the Present Moment. In it, award-winning science author Jo Marchant makes a good case for the likelihood that, in real physical reality, there is no such thing as “now.”

In my own research in creativity, I’ve made a case for the merits of learning to expand your time spent in a flow state. That’s when you’re deeply engaged in some challenging activity, so single-mindedly focused, in fact, that time seems to stop. Which tends to feel mighty pleasant. Could spending more of our time in flow, then, be a kind of perpetual—while flow lasts—state of “now”?

Consider these ideas that were inspired by my reading of In Search of Now:

  1. Learn something new and get good at it. Depending on your personality and time constraints, this may mean first dabbling at a variety of new pursuits, and then, ideally, you’ll choose one and delve deeply into it so that you become very good at it. That's when you no longer have to “think” but allow the thing itself to carry you along. Compare how it feels when you’re writing a first draft and letting the ideas come almost unbidden, to how it feels when you put on your editor’s cap and think hard to come up with the very best way to phrase a thought.
  2. Rearrange your schedule so that you have enough time to stop time. That means, for many of us, that if you avoid flow activities due to too much constraint on the time you have for such intensive sessions, decide what you can give up (animal videos or doom-scrolling, anyone?). Allow yourself the potentially lasting satisfaction of working toward an actual goal.
  3. Don't assume that your perception of time is the only or accurate one. Our brains construct a version of when “now” is, of when exactly the present moment exists. Each of our “right now” moments contains memories of past moments that relate to this one. And such a moment is gone too fast for anything to really happen in it, not to mention that our human brains have been shown by scientists to be very slow at putting together the signals of our senses. Your perceived “now” is already in the recent past.
  4. Remind yourself that what matters most about the “be here now” concept is to give up thoughts of approval by others. Settle into the task you’ve chosen and let the future wait its turn. In a way, you’re stretching out your experience of “now,” which is really the only place anything real can happen.
  5. Be aware in your relationships that others may think differently from you about time. I think of my late husband, who had no problem entering a flow state daily to write poetry, who believed in and trusted the present far more than any future time. Whereas from an early age, I tended to look ahead, always thinking and planning and barely able to recognize, even as a child, that now is where we live. We probably would have had fewer arguments if we had understood on a gut level that such varied ways of understanding “now” are equally valid. Actually, it's possible that such perceptions are somewhat delusional anyway, per current science.
article continues after advertisement

If you’re uncertain what the fuss is about the whole “now” idea, read a book or two to get a better handle on it. I stuck little notes in Marchant’s book, especially in the first half. The philosophy and psychology of the present moment fascinate me, while the latter part of the book focuses more on that whole “quantum physics” weirdness that my mind balks at comprehending.

item.title: Spiritual Bypassing Has a Name; Psychological Bypassing Doesn't
item.description:
Spirituality

Spiritual Bypassing Has a Name; Psychological Bypassing Doesn't

Therapy can be used to avoid the spiritual.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Spiritual bypassing describes using transcendence to avoid psychological pain.
  • The reverse also occurs: clinical language can be used to avoid the numinous.
  • The DSM has had a category for this since 1994; practice has largely not followed.

First article of two parts.

In the early 20th century, Dr. Carl Jung was travelling alone when he was seized by a vision of a monstrous flood covering the lowlands between the North Sea and the Alps, with the drowned bodies of uncounted thousands in the water. At the time, he did not read it as a warning about Europe. He concluded that the material referred to him alone, and that he was perhaps menaced by some form of psychosis. The thought of war, he wrote later, never occurred to him.

Source: Photo by Ihor Frolov on Unsplash

Ten months after this vision, the First World War began.

The founder of depth psychology, a man who would spend the rest of his life arguing that the psyche speaks in symbol and image, first met his own likely numinous material by pathologizing it, interestingly enough. If Jung could do that to himself, the rest of the psychological profession can certainly do it to the people who sit across from them.

Jung wrote extensively on how primary, experiential, and direct psycho-spiritual encounters are the cornerstone of lasting transformation for the human psyche. Yet spirituality can also be misused in ways that quietly prevent growth.

The transpersonal psychotherapist John Welwood gave the field a phrase it badly needed in the mid-1980s. He named the way people in spiritual communities could use meditation, states of transcendence, or the language of oneness to sidestep grief, rage, and the other difficult emotions that arrive when a life falls apart or blows up. He called it spiritual bypassing, and the term has had remarkable staying power.

Wildly enough, we have never named the other direction with anything like the same clarity.

The Bypassing Runs Both Ways

Consider what happens when someone brings an experience they found sacred into a clinical room, particularly when the clinician has no transpersonal, Jungian, or otherwise psycho-spiritually affirming background.

Someone describes a dream that will not release them; it arrived with a quality they struggle to put into words: not a dream about their life, but a dream that seemed to know something. They tell you it changed how they understand their relationship, their dying father, or maybe even their own death. The person is not asking you to believe anything metaphysical, but they are telling you that something important has happened on a deeply spiritual level.

Most skilled therapists will respond with good questions. What might the images represent? What unmet wish or need could the dream be organizing? What emotion or nervous system state sits underneath it? Each of these is a legitimate clinical enquiry, and any one of them could open something important. Yet if the hour ends there, these questions have quietly accomplished something else.

In essence, the clinician has received an experience the person found meaningful and converted it into a symptom of something more real beneath it. The message is rarely explicitly stated and usually lands on some form of: What happened to you is not what happened to you.

I would call this psychological bypassing: the use of clinical or therapeutic language to avoid the numinous, in the same way spiritual bypassing uses transcendent language to avoid the psychological. The direction of travel is identical in both cases; a person moves toward the register they can tolerate and away from the one they cannot.

As far as I can find, the phrase does not appear anywhere in the clinical literature, even though the phenomenon it names has been documented for decades under other headings.

The Field Already Conceded the Point

Here is the part that surprises people: psychiatry formally acknowledged this problem more than thirty years ago.

In 1994, the DSM-IV introduced a category called Religious or Spiritual Problem, under “other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention”. The proposal came from transpersonal clinicians, and it grew directly out of the Spiritual Emergence Network's concern that the mental health system was pathologizing spiritual and religious experiences.

The category survives in the DSM-5, and the manual most often accused of over-diagnosing human experience contains an explicit instruction that some spiritual distress is clearly not a disorder.

Stanislav and Christina Grof continued the argument at greater depth. They fully acknowledged the existence of mental disorders arising from brain dysfunction and the collapse of other bodily systems. However, their claim was that some presentations that look psychotic are better understood as spiritual emergencies, and the treatment implications diverge sharply depending on which one is actually in the room.

Despite all of this, the working assumption in many healthcare settings, and especially in acute ones likes hospitals, is still that mystical experience is psychotic experience until proven otherwise. Curiosity is rare; the spiritual category exists on paper and almost nowhere in the culture of practice, unfortunately.

Why It Is Difficult to Recognize

Spiritual bypassing is comparatively easy to identify because it looks like avoidance. The classic example: Someone will not speak about their marriage ending and keeps saying that everything happens for a reason or it's all part of God's plan. The evasion is legible, particularly when the person refuses any psychological or emotional lens on their own life.

Psychological bypassing, by contrast, looks like rigour. It resembles a clinician doing the work properly: not colluding with a client's defences, not being swept up in the story, holding a psychological frame, and staying grounded or level-headed throughout. Those are real virtues that carry real value, which is precisely what makes this so hard to see in oneself. The interpretive move that reduces an experience to its psychological function is the same move that, twenty minutes later in the same hour, can be exactly what the person needs.

It is also uncomfortable to raise among ourselves, because naming it implies that clinical authority can itself operate as an unconscious defence.

So the question is not whether to interpret. It is whether the explanatory reduction is serving the person in front of us, or protecting the clinician from material they were not trained to hold. Most psychologists and psychotherapists will not know, in the moment, which one we are doing. Noticing that we cannot always tell is where the work starts.

In a second piece to be released soon, I take up what psychological bypassing costs, and what it asks of clinicians in practice. Subscribe to my email list for free to get updates whenever I publish a new article.
